SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm

checks.quote: First, it operates with a fixed task distribution.
One direction is to co-evolve the task distribution by generating new tasks and curricula that adapt to the agent’s capabilities
Second, components of the open-ended exploration loop (e.g., parent selection, evaluation protocols) remain fixed.
Although hyperagents can modify their self-improvement mechanisms, they cannot alter the outer process that determines which agents are selected or how they are evaluated.
Our preliminary results suggest such extensions are feasible (Appendix E.5).
Moreover, evaluation is performed using predefined tasks and metrics, and human oversight is maintained throughout all experiments.
Test tasks are unavailable to the task and meta agents and are used only for final evaluation, which prevents direct test leakage but does not eliminate gaming of the training proxy.

In all other experiments (Section 5), the DGM-H uses a fixed parent selection strategy that is roughly proportional to each agent’s performance score and inversely proportional to the number of its children that successfully compiled (score-child-prop) (Appendix A.2).

While these differences are not statistically significant (p > 0.05), they reveal a consistent qualitative trend: enabling meta-level modification of parent selection yields improvements over random selection, but does not yet surpass a carefully engineered mechanism (Figures 11 and 12).

We measure progress in outer-loop iterations, which count opportunities to generate a new agent rather than a fixed amount of compute, since evolved agents are free to use more or fewer FM calls within each iteration (bounded by a timeout); we report cost estimates in Appendix D.2, and comparing methods under matched compute (e.g., tokens, monetary cost, CPU/GPU usage, wall-clock time) is a natural extension.

In this work, objectives are specified through fixed benchmarks and evaluation criteria. The DGM-H does not alter the underlying task definitions; instead, it optimizes performance with respect to the provided objectives.
After 200 iterations, the best discovered agent achieves a test-set score of 0.700, outperforming ProofAutoGrader’s score of 0.670
